directions: Section I, Part B: Short Answer. Suggested time: 40 minutes (about 13 minutes per question). This part counts for 20 percent of your total score. Answer all three questions. Question 1 provides a secondary source (a historian's account), Question 2 provides a primary source (a document from the time), and Question 3 provides a non-text stimulus (a chart). In your responses, address all parts (A, B, and C) of each question. Use complete sentences; an outline or bulleted list alone is not acceptable.

questions.stimulus: World War I transformed the relationship between Americans and their government. The war gave Washington sweeping new powers to manage the economy, shape public opinion, and punish dissent. The Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a crime to criticize the war effort; Socialist leader Eugene Debs was sentenced to ten years in prison for a speech opposing the war. After the armistice, fear of radicals did not fade: Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer ordered raids that rounded up thousands of suspected communists and anarchists for deportation. Adapted from a secondary account of the World War I home front.

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE way in which World War I expanded the power of the federal government.
parts.B: Briefly explain ONE way in which World War I led to the suppression of dissent in the United States.
parts.C: Briefly explain ONE similarity between the federal government's treatment of dissent during World War I and its treatment of dissent in another period of American history.

exemplar.A: The war led Congress and President Wilson to create agencies that managed the wartime economy on an unprecedented scale, such as the War Industries Board directing factory production and the Food Administration urging conservation, which put the federal government in direct control of economic life.
exemplar.B: The Espionage and Sedition Acts criminalized criticism of the war, and the Supreme Court upheld convictions under them in Schenck v. United States (1919), so opponents of the war such as Eugene Debs were imprisoned for their speeches.
exemplar.C: During the Second Red Scare of the early Cold War, the federal government again traded liberty for security: loyalty programs, HUAC hearings, and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations punished suspected communists much as the Palmer Raids had punished suspected radicals after World War I.

questions.stimulus: "We meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin. Corruption dominates the ballot-box, the Legislatures, the Congress.... The fruits of the toil of millions are badly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few, unprecedented in the history of mankind; and the possessors of these, in turn, despise the Republic and endanger liberty. From the same prolific womb of governmental injustice we breed the two great classes, tramps and millionaires." Source: Ignatius Donnelly, preamble to the People's (Populist) Party platform, Omaha, 1892 (public domain).

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE reason farmers organized into the Populist movement in the late 1800s.
parts.B: Briefly explain how ONE specific demand of the Populists reflected the grievances expressed in the passage.
parts.C: Briefly explain ONE way in which Populist ideas influenced the United States in the years after the movement's decline.

exemplar.A: Farmers were squeezed between falling crop prices and high railroad freight rates and mortgage interest they could not control, so they organized through the Farmers' Alliances and then the People's Party to demand government action.
exemplar.B: The platform's demand for government ownership of the railroads directly answered Donnelly's charge that corrupt alliances between business and government produced 'tramps and millionaires,' by putting the railroads under public control.
exemplar.C: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913), authorizing a federal income tax, enacted the Omaha Platform's graduated income-tax plank, showing Populist ideas living on in Progressive Era reform.

parts.A: Briefly explain ONE way in which the Gold Rush transformed the American West.
parts.B: Briefly explain ONE way in which the Gold Rush affected the development of the United States as a whole.
parts.C: Briefly explain ONE other economic boom in American history and how it transformed a particular region of the United States.

exemplar.A: The Gold Rush filled California with hundreds of thousands of migrants almost overnight, turning San Francisco from a small settlement into a major city and pushing California to statehood in 1850.
exemplar.B: The flood of migrants and wealth intensified the national debate over whether slavery would expand into the new western lands, a debate the Compromise of 1850 tried and failed to settle.
exemplar.C: The early-1900s Texas oil boom transformed the Gulf Southwest: gushers at Spindletop (1901) drew workers and investment, built Houston into an energy capital, and made petroleum the region's defining industry.
